content: To prevent neonatal hypothermia, it is recommended to thoroughly dry newborns after birth. However, this recommendation is based on weak evidence of low quality. Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) is strongly recommended for routine care of newborns weighing 2000 grams or less at birth. It should be initiated in healthcare facilities as soon as the newborns are clinically stable. This recommendation is supported by moderate-quality evidence. For these newborns, continuous KMC is preferred whenever possible. If continuous KMC is not feasible, intermittent KMC is recommended over conventional care. Both recommendations are supported by moderate-quality evidence. Unstable newborns weighing 2000 grams or less, or stable newborns weighing less than 2000 grams who cannot receive KMC, should be cared for in a thermoneutral environment, such as under radiant warmers or in incubators. This is a strong recommendation, but the evidence supporting it is of very low quality. There is insufficient evidence regarding the effectiveness of plastic bags or wraps for thermal care of preterm newborns immediately after birth. However, during stabilization and transfer to specialized neonatal care wards, wrapping preterm newborns in plastic bags or wraps may be considered as an alternative to prevent hypothermia. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence. For preterm babies born at or before 32 weeks of gestation requiring ventilation, it is recommended to start oxygen therapy with 30% oxygen or air (if blended oxygen is unavailable) rather than 100% oxygen. This is a strong recommendation, but the evidence is of very low quality. Progressively higher oxygen concentrations should only be considered if the newborn’s heart rate remains below 60 beats per minute after 30 seconds of adequate ventilation with 30% oxygen or air. This is also a strong recommendation with very low-quality evidence. It should be initiated as soon as the diagnosis is made. These recommendations are supported by low to very low-quality evidence. Surfactant replacement therapy is conditionally recommended for intubated and ventilated newborns with RDS, but only in healthcare facilities equipped with intubation, ventilator care, blood gas analysis, and appropriate nursing and monitoring. Either animal-derived or protein-containing synthetic surfactants can be used. Prophylactic administration of surfactant before the onset of RDS is not recommended. Early administration of surfactant (within the first two hours after birth) is preferred over waiting for symptoms to worsen before initiating rescue therapy. These recommendations are based on moderate to low-quality evidence. Low-birth-weight (LBW) infants, including very low-birth-weight (VLBW) infants, should be fed their mother’s own milk. If this is not possible, donor human milk is recommended in settings where safe and affordable milk-banking facilities are available. If neither option is feasible, standard infant formula should be used. For VLBW infants who fail to gain weight despite adequate feeding with standard formula, preterm infant formula may be considered. These recommendations are based on varying levels of evidence, from moderate to low quality. VLBW infants fed mother’s milk or donor milk do not require bovine milk-based human milk fortifiers unless they fail to gain weight. In such cases, human milk-based fortifiers are preferred. Daily supplementation with calcium (120–140 mg/kg) and phosphorus (60–90 mg/kg) is recommended during the first months of life. Iron supplementation (2–4 mg/kg per day) should begin at two weeks of age and continue until six months. Routine vitamin A or zinc supplementation is not recommended due to insufficient evidence of benefit. These recommendations are based on low to very low-quality evidence. LBW infants should be exclusively breastfed until six months of age. If alternative oral feeding methods are needed, cup or spoon feeding is recommended. Intragastric feeding tubes may be placed via the oral or nasal route based on healthcare provider preference. Feed volumes can be increased by up to 30 ml/kg per day with careful monitoring for feed intolerance. These recommendations are supported by varying levels of evidence, from high to very low quality. For HIV-exposed infants, nucleic acid testing (NAT) at birth can be considered to identify HIV infection. Point-of-care NAT technologies may be used for early infant HIV testing. For children older than 18 months, RDTs can diagnose HIV following national testing strategies. These recommendations are based on low to moderate-quality evidence. Infants born to mothers with HIV who are at high risk of acquiring HIV should receive dual prophylaxis with AZT and NVP for the first six weeks of life, regardless of feeding method. Breastfed infants at high risk should continue prophylaxis for an additional six weeks, using either AZT and NVP or NVP alone. These recommendations are based on moderate to low-quality evidence. Mothers living with HIV should breastfeed for at least 12 months and may continue up to 24 months or longer while receiving full support for antiretroviral therapy (ART) adherence. Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for the first six months of life for HIV-uninfected infants or those with unknown HIV status. These recommendations are supported by low to high-quality evidence. Neonatal seizures lasting more than three minutes or occurring as brief serial seizures should be treated. In facilities with electroencephalography (EEG), all electrical seizures should also be treated, even if not clinically apparent. Hypoglycemia should be ruled out and treated before considering antiepileptic drugs. In cases of suspected sepsis or meningitis, lumbar puncture should be performed, and appropriate antibiotics administered. If lumbar puncture is not feasible, empirical antibiotic treatment should be initiated. Pyridoxine treatment may be considered in specialized centers when no other underlying cause is identified. Phenobarbital is recommended as the first-line treatment for neonatal seizures and should be readily available. If seizures persist despite maximal phenobarbital dosing, midazolam or lidocaine may be used as second-line agents, with lidocaine requiring cardiac monitoring. Antiepileptic drugs can be discontinued if the neonate has been seizure-free for more than 72 hours, and abrupt discontinuation is acceptable if only one drug was used. These recommendations are based on varying levels of evidence. For neonatal jaundice, all newborns should be routinely monitored. Phototherapy should be stopped once bilirubin levels fall below the phototherapy threshold. These recommendations are based on very low-quality evidence. For suspected necrotizing enterocolitis, treatment with intravenous or intramuscular ampicillin (or penicillin) and gentamicin for 10 days is recommended. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. For congenital syphilis, symptomatic or high-risk infants should be treated with aqueous benzyl penicillin or procaine penicillin. Asymptomatic, low-risk infants may be closely monitored or treated with benzathine penicillin G. These recommendations are based on very low-quality evidence. For ophthalmia neonatorum, gonococcal conjunctivitis should be treated with a single dose of intramuscular ceftriaxone, kanamycin, or spectinomycin. Chlamydial conjunctivitis should be treated with oral azithromycin for three days or erythromycin for 14 days. Topical ocular prophylaxis is recommended for all neonates to prevent gonococcal and chlamydial infections. These recommendations are based on low to very low-quality evidence.
